```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Try an editable Shiny app with your own cloud data platform. The console
guide explains where to find the settings, then opens a local app where
you sign in and run a query as yourself. The platform enforces your existing
permissions. Each example starts with a database identity query, so you
don't need to create tables or upload data.

## Choose a platform

| Platform name | Guide and required setup |
| --- | --- |
| `"databricks"` | [Databricks](databricks.html): workspace URL and custom OAuth registration; choose a SQL warehouse after sign-in |
| `"fabric"` | [Microsoft Fabric](fabric.html): SQL server/database and an Entra registration; install fabricQueryR, odbc and Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 |
| `"bigquery"` | [BigQuery](bigquery.html): query project ID and a Google Web OAuth client; no database driver needed |
| `"snowflake"` | [Snowflake](snowflake.html): account server, role, warehouse and a confidential custom OAuth integration; install odbc and the Snowflake ODBC driver |

For example, start the Fabric guide with:

```{r fabric-guide}
shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("fabric")
```

The guide uses `cli` messages and asks only for missing settings. Enter `?`
for help, `back` to revisit a setting, or leave an answer blank to save a
draft for later. It prints a command to resume the same directory.
Account and trial links explain how to arrange access if you have no account
yet; eligibility and organization policies still apply. The guide doesn't
provision cloud resources.

All apps run in local R, without Docker. Sign-in doesn't run SQL; click
**Run example query** when ready. Running queries uses the platform's normal
compute or query allowance. Stop demo ends the local app without stopping
shared cloud services. Edit `app.R` to try different SQL; save and reload
the browser. The non-Databricks apps also copy an editable `demo-ui.R`.

Every platform supports `action = "files"` to create an offline draft.
For scripts, supply the named settings shown in its guide and
`prompt = FALSE`. Settings also use platform-specific environment names,
such as `OAUTHDB_FABRIC_SERVER` or `OAUTHDB_FABRIC_TENANT_ID`.
Secrets use masked input or `OAUTHDB_<PLATFORM>_CLIENT_SECRET`; the launcher
passes them to the child R environment and keeps them out of generated
files. Azure platform names use underscores in environment names.

## Databricks

With shinyOAuthDB installed, install the optional local-app packages:

```{r install}
install.packages(c("brickster", "jsonlite", "processx", "askpass"))
shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("databricks")
```

Run this from the R console. The guide uses `cli` for console messages;
you can enter `?` for help, `back` to revisit a setting or `cancel` to keep
a draft. No Docker is needed. Your R code runs on your computer and uses
your existing cloud workspace.

## Can I use Databricks Free Edition?

Free Edition doesn't provide the account-console or account-level APIs
used to register this custom OAuth app. That blocks this demo's browser
sign-in setup. A full workspace or an eligible full-platform trial needs
access to custom OAuth registration. These are different offerings; see
[Free Edition limits](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/getting-started/free-edition-limitations)
and [free trials](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/getting-started/free-trial).

The guide stops early if you select Free Edition. It doesn't switch to a
shared personal token: the purpose is to demonstrate each Shiny visitor's
own OAuth sign-in and data permissions. To try that flow without a cloud
account, use the [local Docker demos](local-demos.html).

## Find the sign-in settings

| Value | Where to find it |
| --- | --- |
| Workspace URL | Open your workspace and copy its browser address. You can paste the whole URL; the guide keeps only its HTTPS origin. |
| OAuth client ID | Your custom OAuth app registration. The guide can show registration instructions if you don't have one. |
| Client secret | Only for a confidential registration. Enter it through the masked prompt, or provide `OAUTHDB_DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET` in your R environment. |
| Return address | The guide supplies `http://localhost:8100`, or the exact address for your chosen `port`. Register it without adding a slash or path. |

An account administrator creates the registration in **Settings > App
connections** in the Databricks account console. For this SQL example,
allow SQL access. The requested scopes are `openid`, `profile`, `email`,
`offline_access` and `sql`. A public PKCE registration needs no secret;
use one for a local demo when your organization permits it. Follow the
[Databricks registration steps](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/integrations/enable-disable-oauth).

The guide supplies a short request to copy to your administrator. If you
pause, it prints the draft directory and a command for resuming. It never
creates a cloud account, app registration, warehouse or database grant.

If port 8100 is busy, stop the other local app or choose another port:

```{r port}
shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("databricks", port = 8101)
```

That changes the return address to `http://localhost:8101`; update the
app registration to match. The guide never silently changes a registered
callback after sign-in has begun.

## Sign in and choose a warehouse

Click **Sign in** in the local app and use your normal Databricks account.
A SQL warehouse is the compute that runs your SQL. After sign-in, the app
lists visible warehouses by name and state. Pick one you normally use.

If listing fails or is empty, enter a known warehouse ID or HTTP path
from **SQL Warehouses > your warehouse > Connection details**. You can
also supply `warehouse_id` or `http_path` when starting the guide.
Listing a warehouse doesn't prove permission to query it; you need
**CAN USE**, and your own tables also need catalog/schema access and
appropriate table privileges.

Review the query and click **Run example query**:

```sql
SELECT current_user() AS signed_in_user
```

Sign-in and warehouse listing don't open a SQL connection or run this
query. Clicking the button does. Queries can start a stopped warehouse
and consume normal compute credits; see Databricks'
[warehouse behavior](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/sql-warehouse).
Stopping the local demo doesn't stop a shared warehouse or change its
auto-stop settings.

The warehouse stays fixed for that sign-in after the first query. Sign
out and sign in again to choose another one. Sign-out or account changes
clear the previous results and selections. The SQL scope doesn't grant
read-only access: the platform still applies the user's actual privileges.

## Edit the app and resume later

Choose a directory to keep the example, or use the temporary directory
printed by the launcher:

```{r files}
path <- shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("databricks",
  action = "files", path = "my-databricks-demo", prompt = FALSE)
file.edit(file.path(path, "app.R"))
shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("databricks", path = path)
```

`action = "files"` works offline and can create an incomplete draft.
`settings.dcf` stores non-secret settings. Existing `app.R` edits survive
later launches. Change `example_query` to SQL for your own tables, save
the file and reload the browser to try it. **Back to setup** closes the
app and returns to configuration; **Stop demo** ends the local process.

The launcher passes a confidential secret directly through the child
process environment. It doesn't write it to the project, R command
arguments or serialized R files. Tokens stay with shinyOAuth's session
lifecycle. Keep secrets out of `app.R`, `settings.dcf` and source control.

For scripted setup, supply `host`, `client_id`, `client_type` and optionally
`edition`, `warehouse_id` or `http_path`, with `prompt = FALSE`. You can
also supply `OAUTHDB_DATABRICKS_HOST` and `OAUTHDB_DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID`
through the environment. A confidential registration uses the secret
environment variable above. Missing required values produce an error.

## When setup fails

If the workspace check fails, confirm the workspace address and your
network/VPN access and trusted TLS certificates. If sign-in reports a
redirect mismatch, compare the callback exactly with the registration.
An invalid client or scope needs the registration checked; recent
registration changes can take time to apply. Use **Back to setup** to
correct app settings, or resume with the printed directory.

A successful sign-in with a failed query usually needs warehouse or data
permissions checked. Refresh the list or retry the query explicitly when
ready. The demo doesn't automatically replay SQL after failures.

See [Databricks](databricks.html) for the complete client and query APIs,
and [OAuth setup](oauth-setup.html) for the underlying sign-in settings.
